q: What is meant by 'standard cost' in workshop costing?

options.A: The average of the last five years' actual costs
options.B: A predetermined cost of one unit under efficient operating conditions
options.C: The estimated selling price of the finished product
options.D: The lowest cost ever achieved in the shop

q: What does a standard cost card show?

options.A: Only the selling price per unit
options.C: Standard quantity and rate of each cost element per unit of output

q: Standards for material and labour are best set using:

options.A: Time and motion study, past records and engineering estimates
options.B: The lowest price quoted by any supplier
options.C: Workers' own estimates of time required
options.D: Last year's actual costs without adjustment

q: An 'ideal standard' is based on:
An 'attainable standard' differs from an ideal standard because it:

options.B: Allows normal wastage and realistic efficiency
options.C: Is set only for direct material

q: The main purpose of standard costing is:

options.A: Control of costs through comparison of actuals with standards
options.B: Ascertaining the exact historical cost of each job
options.C: Fixing the selling price of railway services

q: Material price variance is computed as:

options.A: Standard price x (standard quantity - actual quantity)
options.B: Actual price x (standard quantity - actual quantity)
options.C: Actual quantity purchased x (standard price - actual price)
options.D: Standard quantity x (standard price - actual price)

q: A favourable material price variance arises when:

options.A: More material is used than standard
options.B: Actual purchase price is below the standard price
options.D: Material is purchased in smaller lots

q: Material usage variance is computed as:

options.A: Actual quantity x (standard price - actual price)
options.C: (Standard quantity - actual quantity) x actual price
options.D: (Standard quantity for actual output - actual quantity used) x standard price

q: An adverse material usage variance may be caused by:

options.A: Excessive wastage, pilferage or substandard material
options.B: A fall in the market price of material

q: Material price variance is normally calculated at the time of purchase because:

options.A: It is easier to compute later
options.C: Price responsibility can be isolated early for prompt action

q: Material mix variance arises when:

options.B: The actual proportion of materials used differs from the standard mix

q: Material yield variance measures:

options.C: The difference between budgeted and actual overhead
options.D: The cost effect of actual output differing from the standard output expected from the input used

q: Labour rate variance is computed as:

options.A: Actual hours paid x (standard rate - actual rate)
options.B: Standard hours x (standard rate - actual rate)
options.C: (Standard hours - actual hours) x actual rate

q: A favourable labour rate variance may arise when:

options.A: Workers take longer than standard time
options.B: Overtime is paid at double rates
options.C: Work is done by lower-paid workers than planned

q: Labour efficiency variance is computed as:

options.A: Actual hours x (standard rate - actual rate)
options.B: (Standard hours for actual output - actual hours worked) x standard rate
options.D: (Actual rate - standard rate) x standard hours

q: An adverse labour efficiency variance can be caused by:

options.D: Poor supervision, machine breakdowns or inferior material

q: Idle time variance is calculated as:

options.A: Idle hours x standard wage rate, normally adverse
options.B: Idle hours x actual wage rate, normally favourable

q: Variable overhead expenditure variance is:

options.B: Actual output minus budgeted output, valued at standard rate
options.C: The difference between actual variable overhead and the budgeted variable overhead for actual hours worked
options.D: Fixed overhead absorbed minus actual fixed overhead

q: Variable overhead efficiency variance is computed as:

options.A: (Actual hours - standard hours) x actual overhead rate
options.B: (Standard hours for actual output - actual hours) x standard variable overhead rate
options.D: Actual hours x (standard rate - actual rate)

q: Fixed overhead expenditure (budget) variance is:

options.A: Absorbed fixed overhead minus actual fixed overhead
options.B: Budgeted output minus actual output, valued at standard rate
options.C: Standard hours minus actual hours, valued at standard rate
options.D: Budgeted fixed overhead minus actual fixed overhead

q: Fixed overhead volume variance arises because:

options.A: Actual production differs from budgeted production

q: Fixed overhead capacity variance measures:

options.A: The effect of price changes on overhead
options.C: Under- or over-utilisation of available capacity, as actual hours differ from budgeted hours
options.D: The difference between variable and fixed overhead

q: Fixed overhead efficiency variance is:

options.A: Budgeted fixed overhead minus actual fixed overhead
options.B: (Standard hours for actual output - actual hours) x standard fixed overhead rate
options.C: Actual hours minus budgeted hours, valued at actual rate

q: Under the two-variance method, fixed overhead variances analysed are:
Under the three-variance method, overhead variances analysed are:

options.C: Rate, efficiency and idle time variances

q: A controllable variance is one which:

options.B: Cannot be influenced by any manager
options.C: Arises from factors within the control of a specified responsibility centre

q: Which of the following is normally an uncontrollable variance?

options.B: A wage increase awarded by a statutory tribunal

q: In practice, variances selected for investigation are:

options.D: Significant variances, judged by size, trend and cost of investigation

q: The principle of 'management by exception' in variance analysis means:

options.A: Management attention is directed only to significant deviations from standards
options.B: Every variance is reported to top management

q: A common rule for investigating a variance is to consider:

options.C: Its size relative to standard cost, its trend, and whether it is controllable
options.D: The colour used in the report

q: Small, routine variances at period end are normally:

options.B: Written off to the costing profit and loss account
options.C: Added to the value of closing stock

q: Variances arising from abnormal, non-recurring causes are:

options.D: Written off to the costing profit and loss account

q: When a variance is traced to an error in the standard itself, the correct action is to:

options.B: Write off the variance and keep the standard

q: Standard costing differs from historical costing mainly because:

options.C: Costs are predetermined before production, whereas historical costing records only actual costs after the event
options.D: It applies only to service industries

q: In a railway workshop, standard cost norms are most useful for:

options.B: Estimating and controlling the cost of POH and IOH overhauls

q: A POH cost norm in a railway workshop specifies:

options.A: The selling price of a coach
options.B: The number of staff on roll
options.D: The standard material, labour hours and overheads for overhauling one coach or wagon

q: Variance analysis applied to workshop job costing helps to:

options.A: Highlight cost overruns on individual jobs for corrective action
options.D: Eliminate the need for time booking

q: In standard costing, overheads are absorbed into production using:

options.A: The actual overhead rate computed at year end

q: If actual overhead exceeds the overhead absorbed at standard rate, the result is:
In standard cost books, a favourable variance is normally recorded as:

options.A: A debit to the variance account
options.C: A charge to the stores ledger
options.D: A credit to the variance account

q: An essential prerequisite for operating standard costing is:

options.A: Standards set for each element of cost and prompt recording of actual costs

q: Standards should be revised when:

options.C: There is a permanent change in methods, prices or technology

q: Standards set too tight may:

options.B: Demotivate workers because targets seem unattainable

q: Responsibility for material price variance usually rests with:
Responsibility for labour efficiency variance usually rests with:
Overhead volume variance is generally regarded as:

options.C: Largely uncontrollable in the short run, as it follows demand and scheduling

q: Sales value variance is:

options.B: The difference between actual sales value and budgeted sales value

q: Sales margin variance (profit variance) measures:

options.D: The effect on profit of actual sales differing from budgeted sales in volume or mix

q: 'Standard cost of actual output' means:

options.A: Actual output valued at the standard cost per unit
options.B: Actual cost of the output produced
options.D: The selling price of actual output

q: A variance is defined as:

options.C: The difference between standard cost and actual cost

q: Variance reports in a workshop are normally prepared:

options.B: Periodically, usually monthly, for timely corrective action

q: 'Standard hours for actual output' are obtained by:

options.B: Multiplying actual hours by the wage rate
options.C: Adding idle time to worked time
options.D: Multiplying actual output by the standard time allowed per unit

q: Under standard costing, finished stock is normally valued at:
Work-in-progress under a standard costing system is valued at:

options.C: Standard cost of the work done

q: A variance caused by using inputs in proportions different from standard, without changing total input quantity, is:
Calendar variance, a sub-variance of capacity variance, arises due to:

options.D: Difference between actual and budgeted working days in the period

q: The efficiency ratio is:

options.A: Standard hours for actual output / actual hours x 100

q: The activity (capacity) ratio is:

options.C: Actual hours worked / budgeted hours x 100

q: The primary objective of variance analysis in a railway workshop is to:

options.B: Locate responsibility for deviations and trigger corrective action for cost control
